As described above, asset classes often move differently from one another. Treasury bonds and cash are among the most “defensive” assets, meaning they may lose less value compared with stocks when the stock market is falling (although some riskier types of bonds, such as high-yield corporate bonds, often behave similarly to stocks). Allocating a portion of your portfolio to defensive assets can help buffer the effects of market volatility.
5. Rebalance your portfolio regularly. [...] “The shorter your time horizon, the more damaging volatility can be,” says Rob Williams, Vice President of Financial Planning at the Schwab Center for Financial Research. “If you need money soon, your capacity to take a risk for a portion of your portfolio is—and should be—lower than if you don’t.” 4. Build in protection against significant volatility. [...] A well-diversified portfolio should help buffer your portfolio from the effects of market volatility. However, you can’t entirely “set it and forget it.” Over time, a portfolio can drift from its target allocation, as some investments do better than others and take up more space in your portfolio. Rebalancing means selling some assets that have performed well and replacing them with other assets that haven’t performed as well, to bring your asset allocation back to its original target.
keyTakeaways: To navigate market volatility, diversify your portfolio, rebalance regularly, and consider defensive assets like bonds.
